summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for generic forward error correction of media, so receivers can rebuild lost packets from extra protection data. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level, and it was replaced by RFC 5109.

eli5.summary: Sending extra backup pieces with a video call lets the receiver patch holes if some pieces get lost on the way.

questions: how does rtp forward error correction work
how does forward error correction work
how can a receiver recover lost packets
subtitle: Extra data packets that let receivers rebuild lost content in real-time streams.

tldr.problem: Real-time media streaming like voice and video cannot retransmit lost packets because retransmission adds unacceptable delay. Some packets arrive damaged or missing.
tldr.mechanism: FEC adds extra protection packets computed by XOR-ing groups of media packets. Each FEC packet encodes information from multiple media packets so that if one media packet is lost, it can be reconstructed from the remaining packets plus the FEC packet.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can recover lost media packets without requesting retransmission, maintaining real-time quality. The RFC was later updated by RFC 5109 with improvements and clarifications.

today: RFC 2733 is a Proposed Standard that was replaced by RFC 5109, which provides clarifications, improvements, and reorganization of the material.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
Real-time multimedia communication over the Internet has historically suffered from packet loss. This is especially true on wide-area connections where congestion is common. Unlike file transfer, real-time applications such as voice and video cannot simply retransmit lost packets because doing so introduces unacceptable delay—a delayed voice packet is useless once the conversation has moved on.

This RFC defines forward error correction (FEC): a technique where the sender transmits extra protection packets alongside the media. These protection packets allow a receiver to rebuild lost media without waiting for a retransmission. The RFC specifies how to format these FEC packets in RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) so they work with any media type and can be combined with media and FEC packets that did arrive.
sections.eli5: If someone drops one of five mail items, they can glue it back together from pieces of the other four plus a backup sheet. FEC is like that backup sheet.

sections.title: How Forward Error Correction Works
sections.content:
FEC is based on a simple operation called XOR (exclusive or), a bitwise mathematical operation. To create a protection packet, the sender takes a group of media packets and applies XOR across all of them. The result is a new packet that encodes information about all the original packets.

The magic of XOR is that if you have all but one of the original packets plus the protection packet, you can recover the missing one by XOR-ing all of them together again. For example, if a sender has packets A, B, and C, it creates protection packet P = A XOR B XOR C. If packet B is lost, the receiver can compute B = A XOR P XOR C.

The RFC allows senders to group packets in many different ways, trading off between recovery ability and network overhead. A simple scheme might protect every two consecutive packets with one FEC packet (50% overhead). A more sophisticated scheme might protect overlapping groups of packets, allowing recovery from multiple consecutive losses at the cost of more FEC packets.
sections.eli5: XOR is like a magic lock: if you lock two things together with XOR, you can unlock one of them with the other. If you XOR three things together, you can recover any one of them if you have the other two.

sections.title: Media and FEC Packet Formats
sections.content:
The RFC specifies two types of packets: unmodified media packets and new FEC packets. Media packets look like normal RTP packets; FEC does not change how media is formatted. This allows non-FEC receivers to ignore FEC entirely and continue using the stream.

An FEC packet contains an RTP header followed by a FEC header (12 bytes) and a FEC payload. The FEC header contains critical fields: a sequence number base indicating the first media packet in the group, a 24-bit mask showing which of the next 24 packets are included in the FEC calculation, a length recovery field that encodes the sum of all protected packet lengths, a payload type recovery field for the media packet types, and a timestamp recovery field. The FEC payload is the XOR of all protected media payloads plus components of the RTP headers.

The 24-bit mask allows an FEC packet to protect any group of up to 24 consecutive packets. This flexibility means a sender can adapt the FEC scheme to changing network conditions without signaling the receiver separately—the receiver can determine what packets are protected just by examining the mask.
sections.eli5: The FEC packet is like a note that says 'I protect packets 1, 3, and 5' (using a mask) and 'if you XOR me with packets 1 and 5, you get packet 3 back.'

sections.title: Recovering Lost Packets
sections.content:
At the receiver, two operations happen. First, the receiver determines which media packets are missing and which combination of received packets and FEC packets can recover them. The RFC does not mandate a specific algorithm for this decision—implementations may choose based on complexity and recovery capability tradeoffs.

Second, once the receiver decides to recover a packet, it follows a precise reconstruction procedure. For each packet (media or FEC) in the recovery group, it constructs a bit string containing specific RTP header fields and the payload, then applies XOR across all of them. This produces a recovery bit string that is decoded back into a complete RTP packet with all header fields and payload intact.

The RFC includes example C code showing a simple recovery algorithm. It maintains a list of FEC packets that have not yet been used and, when a media packet arrives or is recovered, checks whether any pending FEC packets can now be used to recover additional missing packets. This iterative process may recover multiple packets from a single media packet arrival.
sections.eli5: When a piece goes missing, the receiver XORs all the pieces it has—including the backup FEC piece—to magically reconstruct the missing one.

sections.title: Deployment and Signaling
sections.content:
FEC packets are transmitted as a separate RTP stream from media packets. They may be sent on a different port, multicast group, or SSRC (synchronization source), depending on the application. The RFC describes how to signal FEC usage using SDP (Session Description Protocol), the standard way to negotiate multimedia sessions.

When FEC is sent as a separate stream, SDP uses a dynamic payload type marked as parityfec and includes an fmtp attribute specifying where the FEC is sent. The RFC also shows how to combine FEC with the redundant encodings payload format (RFC 2198), where FEC becomes a secondary codec packaged with the media in a single RTP packet.

FEC can also be used with RTSP (Real Time Streaming Protocol), where the same signaling mechanisms apply. The RFC includes security considerations around encryption: if both media and FEC are encrypted, they should use the same key to avoid the complexity of managing different keys, though applications must be aware that changing encryption keys requires care when FEC packets span the key change boundary.
sections.eli5: The sender tells the receiver 'FEC packets are coming to this address on this port' using a setup message. Then both sides know how to find and use the backup pieces.
